To summarize what turn calming is, it's intended to reduce turning speeds, particularly to eliminate the highest speed turns, and to increase driver visibility of pedestrians in the crosswalk by reorienting the vehicle to be looking straight ahead at the crosswalk rather than at an angle.

And it's typically implemented through a quick build program. So the cities who have successfully implemented it, including New York, Portland, San Francisco, Toronto. They have all used a quick build program, and I'll show you some different images of what quick build could look like versus a more long-term program. most of these cities have implemented left turn calming, which we'll talk about, as well as some of them have implemented right turn calming. So left turn calming is primarily using a hardened center line or a small median bump along the center line of the roadway at the intersection. This can be with or without flexible posts and with or without a nose extension. I'll go into more detail about that in a moment. Right turn calming can include a slow turn wedge. That would be a quick build solution that I'll talk about, as well as a truck apron or pillow, which is more of a long-term solution. And then pavement striping with or without flexible posts, again, quick build

or timing considerations that signalize intersections, which would include a leading pedestrian interval with a no turn on red. We looked at a study primarily coming out of Portland that looked at how their hardened center lines were in effectiveness at their primary goals, which were to decrease turning speeds and decrease the drivers crossing the center line.

So the first image on this slide shows a hardened center line without flexible posts with a nose extension. That means that the hardened center line goes past the crosswalk into the intersection. And those saw the highest decrease in turning speeds at 16% and the highest decrease in drivers crossing the center line at 90 to 100%.

Without the nose extension, we saw a slight decrease in each of those statistics as shown. And the second image shows an example from Washington, D.C., where they have a hardened center line without it going into the intersection past the crosswalk. This was a smaller study group, but they did find that, again, with the nose extension, They had similar results, and without the nose extension, slightly higher proportion of drivers who were not crossing the center line. They're more likely to be struck and knocked down and need replacing with the flexible posts. So as an example, the New York City DOT is moving away from using these because of that cost and lack of increase in effectiveness. Right turn calming measures as a quick build include a corner wedge, which is the same type of temporary curbing material that's put into the corner to encourage drivers to go around it.

And then this design must consider the path of the bicyclist if there's a bike lane especially because they can be pretty hazardous to bicyclists who have to traverse over them. There's also a design called a truck pillow or an apron.
